title: Retrieval Quality
scopeHtml: Scope: Hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting, HyDE, filters, multi-hop and graph approaches.

notes.title: Hybrid search
notes.html:
Why dense retrieval alone is not enough. Embeddings capture meaning but blur exact tokens: product codes ("XJ-4471"), error messages, names, acronyms, version numbers, rare technical terms, negations and numbers. Keyword search (BM25) is the opposite: precise on exact terms, blind to paraphrase and synonyms.

BM25 in short. A probabilistic ranking function over an inverted index: score(term) = IDF(term) × (tf × (k1+1)) / (tf + k1 × (1 − b + b × doclen/avglen)). Rewards rare query terms (IDF), saturates term frequency, normalizes by document length. Fast, explainable, no training.

Hybrid search runs both retrievers in parallel and fuses their ranked lists.

Fusion methods.

  • Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i(d)) with k ≈ 60 across the lists. No score normalization needed; robust default.
  • Weighted score fusion: normalize scores (min-max or z-score) and combine α·dense + (1−α)·sparse; tune α on your eval.
  • Learned sparse retrievers (SPLADE) and multi-vector (ColBERT) are further options bridging both worlds.

Tuning. Evaluate dense-only, BM25-only, and hybrid on a labelled set with recall@k/nDCG; hybrid is usually best on enterprise/technical corpora. Query analysis can route: identifier-looking queries lean lexical; natural-language questions lean semantic.

Implementation notes. Many stores support hybrid natively (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant, Vespa, Postgres full-text + pgvector). Use language-appropriate analyzers (stemming, stopwords, tokenization for CJK), field boosts (title > body), and phrase/boolean filters.

Real life. Searching a shop by description ("red running shoes") and by SKU ("RX-4471"); you want both to work.

notes.title: Reranking
notes.html:
Two-stage retrieval. Stage 1 (fast, recall-oriented): bi-encoder and/or BM25 retrieve 50 to 200 candidates. Stage 2 (slow, precision-oriented): a cross-encoder reranker reads each (query, candidate) pair together and outputs a relevance score; keep the top 3 to 10 for the prompt.

Why it helps. Query and passage attend to each other, capturing negation, conditions, exact constraints and answerability that vector similarity misses. Typical gains: +5 to 20 points of precision@k or nDCG; also improves context quality, reducing prompt tokens.

Options. Open cross-encoders (bge-reranker, MiniLM-based), hosted reranker APIs (Cohere Rerank, Voyage), late-interaction models (ColBERT), or LLM-based reranking (listwise/pointwise prompts; powerful but costly and slower).

Costs and controls. Latency scales with candidates × length: 100 candidates × 512 tokens can be 100 to 400 ms on a GPU. Mitigate: cap candidates, truncate passages, batch on GPU, cache scores for repeated queries, use smaller rerankers, apply rerank only when needed (e.g. low first-stage confidence).

Thresholding. Reranker scores are better calibrated than raw cosine: use a threshold (or a gap between top scores) to decide "not enough evidence" and let the model answer "I don't know" or ask a clarifying question.

Evaluation. Measure with and without reranking on recall@k, nDCG@k, and end-answer quality; check latency budget impact.

Real life. Shortlisting CVs by headline, then interviewing the shortlist.

notes.title: Query transformation
notes.html:
The problem. User questions are poor search queries: elliptical in multi-turn chat ("and for Europe?"), multi-part, vague, using different vocabulary than the documents.

Techniques.

  • Conversational rewriting: an LLM turns the latest message plus history into a standalone query.
  • Query expansion: add synonyms/related terms (for BM25) or generate multiple paraphrases (multi-query) and merge results (RRF).
  • Decomposition: split a complex question into sub-questions, retrieve for each, then synthesize (sequential for dependent ones).
  • HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings): have the model write a hypothetical answer, embed that, and retrieve real passages similar to it; bridges the query-document style gap, but can inject model hallucinations into the search.
  • Step-back prompting: ask a more general question to retrieve background principles.
  • Intent classification/routing: decide which index, tool, or strategy fits (FAQ vs docs vs database).
  • Metadata extraction: parse filters from the query ("invoices from March 2025 for Acme") and apply them as structured filters (self-querying retriever).
  • Spelling/acronym normalization using a glossary.

Trade-offs. Each LLM-based transform adds latency (200 ms to 2 s) and cost, and can introduce drift from the user's intent. Use selectively, measure the gain on the eval, and fall back to the raw query if transformation fails.

Real life. A librarian who asks a clarifying question or rephrases your request before searching the stacks.

notes.title: Metadata filtering and access control
notes.html:
Filters improve relevance and efficiency. Restrict by document type, product, version, language, date range, region, tenant, or source system before or during vector search.

Access control (security-critical).

  • Store ACL metadata (user, group, role, tenant ids) with each chunk; sync permission changes from the source system.
  • Enforce at query time inside the retrieval layer by applying the requesting user's identity as a filter. Never retrieve everything and rely on the LLM to withhold restricted text.
  • Prefer separate indexes/namespaces per tenant for strong isolation, or filtered single indexes with tested guarantees.
  • Consider document-level and chunk-level permissions; handle revocation delays and cached results.
  • Log which documents were used for each answer (audit).
  • Test with canary documents: a user without access must never see them in results, citations, or error messages.

Technical pitfalls. Post-filtering ANN results can return fewer than k (or zero) when filters are selective; use index-native filtering and evaluate recall under realistic filters. Filter cardinality, index design (partitioning by tenant), and filter-aware ANN parameters matter at scale.

Freshness filters/boosts. Boost recent documents, exclude superseded versions, or filter on status = "published".

Real life. A records office that only fetches the files your badge allows.

notes.title: Multi-hop and graph approaches
notes.html:
Multi-hop questions need several pieces of evidence connected by reasoning: "Which team owns the service that caused last week's outage, and who is its on-call?" Single-shot retrieval seldom finds all pieces.

Approaches.

  • Iterative / agentic retrieval: the model retrieves, reasons about what's missing, issues a new query, repeats until sufficient or a step limit. Flexible; costlier and less predictable; log each step.
  • Decomposition + sequential retrieval (see query transformation).
  • Knowledge graphs / GraphRAG: extract entities and relations from the corpus into a graph; retrieve by traversing relationships and community summaries; strong for corpus-wide "global" questions ("What are the main themes?") and relationship queries; expensive to build and keep fresh; extraction errors propagate.
  • Hierarchical retrieval / RAPTOR: build a tree of summaries; retrieve at the right level of abstraction.
  • Text-to-SQL / API tools for structured data joins.

When to adopt. Only when evaluation shows single-hop hybrid + rerank failing on a significant class of real questions. Complexity must pay for itself.

Real life. Following footnotes from one paper to the next until you find the original source.

notes.title: Chunking strategies beyond fixed size
notes.html:
Semantic chunking. Embed sentences, split where similarity between adjacent sentences/windows falls below a threshold or where topic shifts; yields coherent chunks of variable length. Costs extra embedding compute and tuning.

Parent-document retrieval. Index small chunks (precise matching) but return their larger parent section (rich context). Reduces fragmentation without diluting embeddings.

Sentence-window retrieval. Match single sentences, return window of ±N sentences.

Contextual retrieval. Prepend LLM-generated context to each chunk ("This chunk is from the 2024 refund policy, section on opened items…") before embedding and BM25 indexing; reported to cut retrieval failures substantially at modest preprocessing cost (prompt caching makes it cheap).

Proposition/atomic-fact chunking. Rewrite text into self-contained statements; high precision, more chunks.

Late chunking / long-context embedding models. Embed the whole document with a long-context model, then pool token embeddings per chunk, preserving cross-chunk context.

Multi-representation indexing. Index summaries, hypothetical questions, or keywords that point to the original chunk.

Evaluate chunking like any hyperparameter: sweep sizes/strategies against your labelled retrieval set; there is no universal best.

Real life. Finding the paragraph, then reading the whole page around it.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Hybrid search. Dense retrieval handles meaning, BM25 handles exact terms; fuse with RRF (k≈60) or tuned weights; hybrid is the strong default for technical and enterprise content.

Reranking. Retrieve 50 to 200, rerank with a cross-encoder to the top 3 to 10: bigger precision, better prompts, calibrated thresholds; budget the latency (100 to 400 ms) and cap candidates.

Query transformation. Rewrite using history, expand/multi-query, decompose, HyDE, step-back, route by intent, extract metadata filters. Each adds latency and risk; adopt based on eval gains.

Filtering and security. Use metadata filters and enforce permissions in the retrieval layer; test isolation with canaries; avoid post-filter recall collapse by using index-native filtering.

Multi-hop. Iterative/agentic retrieval, decomposition, GraphRAG/hierarchical summaries for relational or corpus-wide questions — use only when single-hop fails measurably.

Chunking upgrades. Semantic, parent-document, sentence-window, contextual (LLM-added context), propositions, late chunking, multi-representation; tune empirically.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Dense for meaning, sparse for exact terms, fuse with RRF."
  • "Retrieve wide, rerank narrow."
  • "Enforce ACLs in the retriever, never in the prompt."
  • "Add multi-hop machinery only after the eval shows single-hop is the bottleneck."

questions.promptHtml: We already have a vector search over our docs. Why would anyone add keyword search next to it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know what embeddings are bad at, not just that "hybrid is better".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A vector search turns text into a list of numbers (an embedding) so that similar meanings land close together. That is great for paraphrases but blurry for exact tokens: product codes like "XJ-4471", error messages, names, version numbers, negations. Keyword search (BM25) is the reverse: exact on rare terms, blind to synonyms. Running both and merging the results covers both failure modes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An embedding model compresses a whole passage into a fixed-size vector, so a rare token like "XJ-4471" contributes little to the final point. Two different SKUs look almost the same to it. BM25 works on an inverted index (word to list of documents) and gives a high weight to rare words, so the exact SKU wins immediately.

query "error E1234 on login"
dense : finds "login failures" articles (right topic, wrong error code)
BM25  : finds the page that literally contains E1234
hybrid: both appear in the fused top-k

Cost of hybrid: two indexes (or a store supporting both), a fusion step, and one more thing to tune. Gain: usually the largest cheap recall improvement on technical or enterprise corpora. Always verify on your own labelled queries: compare dense-only, BM25-only and hybrid on recall@k.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding hybrid without measuring; on a purely conversational corpus the gain may be small.
  • Using the default English analyzer on code, identifiers or other languages, so tokens are split or stemmed wrongly.
  • Believing a bigger embedding model removes the need for lexical search.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Give a query where BM25 loses to dense. → "How do I get my money back?" vs a page titled "Refund policy"; no shared words.
  2. Give one where dense loses. → "ERR_CONN_4471" or "version 2.3.1 changelog".
  3. Does the answer change with a multilingual corpus? → Yes: analyzers per language, and a multilingual embedding model; lexical match is weaker across languages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "hybrid combines meaning and keywords." Senior: names the failure classes, says to measure on a labelled set per query type, and considers routing identifier-like queries lexical-first.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot could not find articles for exact error codes until BM25 was fused in; recall@10 on code queries went from near zero to usable.

questions.promptHtml: Explain BM25 to someone who has never seen it. What do IDF, term frequency saturation and length normalization each do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: BM25 is the lexical baseline every retrieval system should beat or combine with.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: BM25 scores a document for a query by summing a score per query word. Each word score rewards rare words (IDF), rewards repeats but with diminishing returns (saturation, controlled by k1), and penalizes long documents (normalization, controlled by b). It needs no training, runs on an inverted index and is easy to explain.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Formula per term: IDF(t) * tf*(k1+1) / (tf + k1*(1 - b + b*doclen/avglen)).

  • IDF: a word in nearly every document ("the") says nothing; a word in 3 of 1M documents is a strong signal.
  • Saturation: the 10th occurrence of a word adds much less than the 2nd. With k1 around 1.2 to 2 the score flattens quickly.
  • Length normalization: a word appearing twice in a 50-word chunk is more telling than twice in a 5,000-word page. b=0 turns it off, b=1 is full normalization (typical default about 0.75).

An inverted index maps each word to the documents containing it, so only documents sharing a query word are scored. This is why BM25 is milliseconds even on millions of documents.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting analyzers: stemming, lowercasing, stopwords change scores a lot.
  • Comparing BM25 scores across queries; they are only meaningful for ranking within a query.
  • Tuning k1 and b without an eval set.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not plain TF-IDF? → TF grows linearly and ignores length; BM25 saturates and normalizes.
  2. Can BM25 find synonyms? → No, unless you expand the query or use a learned sparse model such as SPLADE.
  3. Does chunk size affect BM25? → Yes, through length normalization and IDF statistics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "keyword scoring with TF-IDF." Senior: explains each parameter's effect, analyzer choices, and why raw scores cannot be mixed directly with cosine.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved to 200-token chunks and BM25 quality dropped because titles were no longer in every chunk; they added a title field with a boost.

questions.promptHtml: What is reranking in a RAG pipeline, and why not just retrieve the top 5 directly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The "retrieve wide, rerank narrow" pattern is the most common quality lever in production RAG.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: First stage is fast and cheap: vector and/or keyword search returns maybe 100 candidates, optimizing recall. Second stage is a cross-encoder, a model that reads the query and one candidate together and outputs a relevance score. I keep the top 5 by that score. It is slower but much more precise, so it is only used on the shortlist.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search is fast, but the two texts never "see" each other. A cross-encoder feeds [query][document] through one transformer, so attention connects words across both: it notices negation, conditions ("only for EU customers") and whether the passage answers the question. It cannot be precomputed, so cost is candidates x length.

corpus 10M chunks --ANN/BM25--> 100 candidates --cross-encoder--> top 5 --> LLM prompt

Benefits: higher precision@k, fewer irrelevant tokens in the prompt (cheaper, less distraction), scores that support a threshold.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
ce = CrossEncoder("BAAI/bge-reranker-base")  # verify model id in HF
def rerank(q, cands, k=5):
    s = ce.predict([(q, c) for c in cands])
    return [c for _, c in sorted(zip(s, cands), reverse=True)][:k]
// Rerankers are usually a separate service; Kotlin calls it over HTTP.
interface Reranker { fun score(query: String, docs: List<String>): List<Double> }

fun rerank(r: Reranker, q: String, cands: List<String>, k: Int = 5): List<String> =
    cands.zip(r.score(q, cands)).sortedByDescending { it.second }.take(k).map { it.first }
// Same idea: Reranker is a client for a hosted or self-run rerank endpoint.
interface Reranker { List<Double> score(String query, List<String> docs); }

static List<String> rerank(Reranker r, String q, List<String> cands, int k) {
    List<Double> s = r.score(q, cands);
    return java.util.stream.IntStream.range(0, cands.size()).boxed()
        .sorted((a, b) -> Double.compare(s.get(b), s.get(a)))
        .limit(k).map(cands::get).toList();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reranking only 10 candidates, so the right chunk was never in the pool.
  • Feeding very long passages and paying latency for nothing.
  • Skipping the before/after measurement.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use the cross-encoder on the whole corpus? → Cost is linear in corpus size per query; impossible at millions of chunks.
  2. How many candidates? → Tune; 50 to 200 is a typical range, bounded by latency budget.
  3. Can an LLM be the reranker? → Yes (pointwise/listwise prompts), stronger but slower and costlier.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "reranker improves ordering." Senior: separates recall (stage 1) from precision (stage 2), budgets latency, and uses scores for thresholds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Adding a reranker on 100 candidates lifted nDCG@5 noticeably and let the prompt shrink from 10 to 4 chunks.

questions.subtopic: Reciprocal rank fusion vs weighted fusion
questions.promptHtml: You have a ranked list from BM25 and another from vector search. How do you merge them, and what are the trade-offs of RRF versus weighted score fusion?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that scores from different retrievers live on different scales.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: BM25 scores are unbounded and cosine scores sit between roughly 0 and 1, so adding them raw is meaningless. Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores scores and uses only ranks: score(d) = sum 1/(k + rank) with k about 60. It is a robust default with nothing to tune. Weighted fusion normalizes scores then mixes with alpha; it can beat RRF when tuned on an eval set but is sensitive to score distributions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RRF: a document ranked 1st in both lists gets 2/61; one that is 1st in one list and absent in the other gets 1/61. The k constant dampens the advantage of rank 1 over rank 2, so agreement across lists matters more than a single top spot.

Weighted: min-max or z-score normalize each list per query, then alpha*dense + (1-alpha)*sparse. Problem: min-max depends on the best and worst in that particular result list, so the same document can get different scores query to query, and one outlier squashes everything else.

Choose RRF first; move to weighted (or a learned fusion/reranker) only if the eval shows a gain. A reranker after fusion usually matters more than the fusion choice.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def rrf(lists, k=60):
    s = {}
    for lst in lists:
        for rank, d in enumerate(lst, 1):
            s[d] = s.get(d, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(s, key=s.get, reverse=True)
fun rrf(lists: List<List<String>>, k: Int = 60): List<String> {
    val s = mutableMapOf<String, Double>()
    for (lst in lists) lst.forEachIndexed { i, d -> s.merge(d, 1.0 / (k + i + 1), Double::plus) }
    return s.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.map { it.key }
}
static List<String> rrf(List<List<String>> lists, int k) {
    Map<String, Double> s = new HashMap<>();
    for (List<String> lst : lists)
        for (int i = 0; i < lst.size(); i++)
            s.merge(lst.get(i), 1.0 / (k + i + 1), Double::sum);
    return s.entrySet().stream()
        .sorted((a, b) -> Double.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()))
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Summing raw BM25 and cosine scores.
  • Using 0-based ranks and getting a divide-style off-by-one inconsistency across code paths.
  • Fusing lists of very different length without capping each at the same depth.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you weight RRF? → Yes, multiply each list's contribution; tune on eval.
  2. What if one retriever returns nothing? → RRF degrades gracefully to the other list.
  3. When is weighted better? → When score magnitude carries signal (strong confidence gap) and you have data to tune alpha.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "average the scores." Senior: explains scale mismatch, picks RRF as a baseline, and validates against a labelled set.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-tuned alpha worked in March and broke after an embedding model upgrade shifted score distributions; RRF did not need retuning.

questions.promptHtml: A user asks "How much is the Pro plan?" then follows with "and for Europe?". Why does retrieval fail on the second message and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Multi-turn chat is the default product shape; naive RAG embeds only the last message.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "And for Europe?" has no topic on its own, so its embedding matches nothing useful. I use a small LLM call to rewrite the latest message plus recent history into a standalone query: "Pro plan price in Europe". Then I retrieve with that. I keep the original as a fallback if the rewrite fails.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Retrieval is stateless: the index sees only the query text. Follow-ups use pronouns and ellipsis ("it", "that one", "and for Europe"). Rewriter prompt: give last N turns, ask for a self-contained question, no answering, keep entities and numbers verbatim. Use a small fast model; the cost is roughly 200 to 800 ms and a few hundred tokens.

Safeguards: cap history length, instruct "if already standalone, return unchanged", log both versions, and run rewrite and raw query retrieval in parallel then fuse if latency matters.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Embedding the whole chat history as the query, which dilutes the signal.
  • Letting the rewriter answer or add facts.
  • Not logging the rewritten query, making failures impossible to debug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the rewrite drifts? → Compare with the raw query results; evaluate rewrite quality on a labelled multi-turn set.
  2. Does the generator also get the history? → Yes, the final answer prompt still includes the conversation.
  3. Cheaper alternative? → Concatenate last user turn with the previous one; works for simple cases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "rewrite the question with an LLM." Senior: adds guardrails, fallback, logging, a multi-turn eval set, and latency budget.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Follow-up questions had 30 percent lower hit rate than first questions until a rewrite step was added.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a cross-encoder more accurate than a bi-encoder, and why can't we use it as our first-stage retriever?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests the mechanism, not just the pattern, and the compute reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bi-encoder encodes query and document separately into vectors and compares them, so documents can be encoded once, offline. A cross-encoder reads both together in one pass with full attention between them, so it judges relevance more precisely, but nothing can be precomputed: each query needs one forward pass per candidate. That is fine for 100 candidates and impossible for 10 million.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Bi-encoder cost: one query forward pass plus an ANN lookup (sub-linear in corpus size). Cross-encoder cost: N forward passes of length (query + doc). For N=100 and 512 tokens each, that is about 51k tokens through a transformer per query; on a GPU, 100 to 400 ms is typical (verify on your hardware).

Why more accurate: interaction. "Does the policy cover opened items?" versus a passage saying "unopened items only" differ by one word that a pooled vector averages away, but token-level cross attention can catch.

Middle ground: late interaction (ColBERT) stores per-token vectors and does cheap token-level matching: more accurate than a bi-encoder, cheaper than a cross-encoder, but larger index.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking a cross-encoder produces an embedding you can store.
  • Ignoring max sequence length: long chunks get truncated silently.
  • Assuming a bigger reranker is always worth the latency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is ColBERT? → Multi-vector late interaction, between the two designs.
  2. Can you distill a cross-encoder? → Yes, train a bi-encoder on its labels to improve stage one.
  3. How would you reduce reranker cost? → Cap candidates, truncate, batch, cache, smaller model, skip when stage one is confident.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cross-encoder is more accurate but slower." Senior: quantifies cost, explains the interaction mechanism, and names the middle options.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Swapping a large reranker for a small one cut p95 by 150 ms with a minor nDCG loss, which the team accepted.

questions.promptHtml: Where and how should user permissions be enforced in a RAG system? Why not just tell the LLM not to reveal restricted content?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A data leak is the worst RAG failure, and prompt-based security is a classic mistake.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Permissions must be enforced in the retrieval layer, before any text reaches the model. Each chunk stores access metadata (user, group, tenant ids); each query applies the caller's identity as a filter inside the vector search. If restricted text never enters the prompt, it cannot be leaked, whereas "please don't reveal" can be bypassed by prompt injection or a plain model mistake.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pipeline: ingest copies ACLs from the source system (Drive, SharePoint, Confluence) onto each chunk; a sync job propagates permission changes and deletions. Query time: resolve the user's groups from the identity provider (trusted server side, never from the client request body), then pass filter = tenant == X AND (acl_groups IN user_groups) into the vector DB query. Use index-native filtering, not filtering the returned results afterward.

Isolation levels: separate collections per tenant (strongest, more operational overhead) or one index with filters (cheaper, needs testing). Also protect caches (a semantic cache keyed only by query text can serve one user's answer to another), citations and error messages. Keep an audit log of chunk ids used per answer.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Taking the user id or role from a field the client can edit.
  • Caching answers without the permission scope in the key.
  • Forgetting revocation delay: a user is removed from a group but chunks keep old ACLs for hours.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test it? → Canary documents: a user without access must never see them in results, citations or errors.
  2. Document-level vs chunk-level ACLs? → Chunk-level inherits from the document unless sections have their own permissions.
  3. What about the LLM's tool calls? → Tools must apply the same user-scoped authorization.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "filter by user id." Senior: ties it to identity trust, ACL sync, cache keys, tenant isolation tier, and canary tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An HR assistant leaked salary bands because ACLs were synced nightly and a revoked manager still had access for up to 24 hours.

questions.contextHtml: An internal IT-helpdesk RAG bot runs dense-only retrieval over 400k chunks (top-5, bge-style embeddings). Users complain: "VPN error 809 on Windows" returns generic VPN setup pages, while page "KB-2217: Error 809 fix" exists. A sample of 200 logged queries shows 60 contain error codes or ticket ids; on those, the right page appears in the top-5 only 35 percent of the time versus 82 percent for plain-language queries. Embedding model and chunking were unchanged for months.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a bigger embedding model" or "increase top-k to 20". It treats a lexical-match problem as a semantics problem and bloats the prompt.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the KB-2217 chunk actually indexed with the code in its text (ingestion check)? What is the store (does it support BM25)? Latency budget? Do we have labelled queries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Regex-detect error codes and ticket ids and do an exact-match lookup on a metadata/keyword field, pinning that hit into the results.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) dense models blur rare tokens (most likely, the split by query type points to it); (b) chunk with the code was split from its title; (c) tokenization of "809" is weak; (d) index stale (red herring: other queries are fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the 60 code queries against BM25-only and see the hit rate; inspect the chunk text; check the index timestamp.
  5. Root cause: Embeddings compress meaning and give little weight to a short numeric token; BM25 would weigh the rare "809" heavily through IDF.
  6. Fix: Short-term: the regex pin. Long-term: hybrid BM25 + dense with RRF, a code-friendly analyzer (do not split alphanumerics), then a reranker on top 50.
  7. Prevention: Segment eval by query type (code vs natural language), track hit rate per segment, alert on regression.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise top-k (prompt cost, distraction) nor re-embed the corpus before testing the cheaper lexical fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• BM25 now matches "809" in unrelated pages mentioning port 809. → Fusion plus reranker, and boost the title field.
  • The store has no BM25. → Add a separate engine or use Postgres full-text beside pgvector; fuse in the app.
  • Latency grew 80 ms. → Run both retrievals in parallel; the cost is the max, not the sum.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support team spent two weeks fine-tuning embeddings for error codes before someone tried plain BM25 on the failed queries; it solved 90 percent of them in an afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only a larger model or larger top-k.
  • Hire: identifies the lexical gap, proposes hybrid, measures by segment.
  • Strong hire: adds quick mitigation, analyzer details, fusion, reranker, per-segment monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: What is HyDE, when does it help, and what can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of the query-document style gap and of hallucination risk inside retrieval.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) asks an LLM to write a fake answer to the question, then embeds that fake answer and searches with it. A short question looks different from a long document passage, but a made-up answer looks like one, so it lands closer to real passages. It helps with vague or short queries; the risk is that the invented answer contains wrong facts that steer retrieval to the wrong place.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flow: query -> LLM writes a plausible paragraph (not shown to the user) -> embed the paragraph -> vector search -> real passages go to the final answer. The fake text is only a search key; the final answer must be grounded in the retrieved real documents.

Works when the corpus uses domain wording that the user does not (the LLM supplies the vocabulary). Hurts when the model lacks the domain knowledge (private product names), when the question is already specific, or for exact lookups. Adds an LLM call (about 0.5 to 2 s). Mitigation: embed both the query and the hypothetical text and fuse the results; evaluate on a labelled set before shipping.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Showing or trusting the hypothetical answer as a source.
  • Using HyDE on identifier queries.
  • Adopting it without an A/B on recall@k.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. HyDE vs multi-query? → Multi-query makes paraphrased questions; HyDE makes an answer-shaped document.
  2. How to limit drift? → Fuse with raw-query results.
  3. Does it work for private jargon? → Poorly, the LLM has not seen it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "generate a fake answer and embed it." Senior: states when it fails, fuses with the raw query, and measures it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: On a medical-style corpus HyDE improved recall for lay-language questions but returned wrong drug sections for rare brand names.

questions.promptHtml: Small chunks match precisely but lack context; large chunks have context but match poorly. How do you get both?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The chunk size trade-off is the central tuning problem in RAG.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Index small pieces for matching, but return a bigger surrounding unit to the model. In parent-document retrieval, I embed small child chunks (say 200 tokens) that each point to a parent section (say 1,500 tokens); when a child matches, I send the parent. Sentence-window retrieval does the same with a single sentence plus or minus N neighbors.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A small chunk has one topic, so its embedding is sharp. But the answer often needs the paragraph around it. Store child_id -> parent_id, keep parents in a document store, dedupe when several children share a parent, and cap total prompt tokens.

Risks: bigger context means more tokens and noise; two matching children from one parent should merge, not duplicate. Tune child and parent sizes on your eval, not by default.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def expand(hits, parents, budget=3000):
    out, seen, used = [], set(), 0
    for h in hits:                      # hits sorted best-first
        pid = h["parent_id"]
        if pid in seen: continue
        text = parents[pid]
        if used + len(text) > budget: break   # chars as a rough proxy; use tokens in prod
        seen.add(pid); out.append(text); used += len(text)
    return out
fun expand(hits: List<Hit>, parents: Map<String, String>, budget: Int = 3000): List<String> {
    val seen = mutableSetOf<String>(); val out = mutableListOf<String>(); var used = 0
    for (h in hits) {
        if (!seen.add(h.parentId)) continue
        val t = parents.getValue(h.parentId)
        if (used + t.length > budget) break
        out += t; used += t.length
    }
    return out
}
static List<String> expand(List<Hit> hits, Map<String, String> parents, int budget) {
    Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(); List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); int used = 0;
    for (Hit h : hits) {
        if (!seen.add(h.parentId())) continue;
        String t = parents.get(h.parentId());
        if (used + t.length() > budget) break;
        out.add(t); used += t.length();
    }
    return out;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning duplicate parents.
  • No token budget, so one huge parent eats the prompt.
  • Forgetting to update parents when documents change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Parent-document vs larger chunks? → Larger chunks dilute the embedding; this keeps matching sharp.
  2. How does it affect reranking? → Rerank children (precise) then expand, or rerank parents; test both.
  3. Where do headings go? → Store them in metadata or prepend to children.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "match small, return big." Senior: handles dedup, budgets, updates, and the rerank interaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Contract Q&A answers were cut mid-clause until parents replaced 256-token chunks in the prompt.

questions.contextHtml: A RAG endpoint has p95 latency 2.4 s against a 1.5 s target. Breakdown: query embedding 60 ms, vector+BM25 search 90 ms, cross-encoder reranking of 200 candidates (about 450 tokens each) 1,100 ms on one shared GPU, LLM generation 1,000 ms. Traffic is 40 QPS at peak. Removing the reranker drops answer-correctness from 0.81 to 0.72 on the eval set. GPU utilization is 95 percent at peak.
questions.promptHtml: How do you hit the target without losing most of the quality?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the reranker" or "buy a bigger GPU", with no measurement of how many candidates are needed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does the right chunk typically rank in stage one (recall@20 vs @200)? Are passages truncated? Is streaming allowed (time to first token)? Repeated queries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut candidates 200 to 50 and truncate to 256 tokens; that is roughly 8x less work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most relevant chunks are in top 50 already; (b) GPU queuing at peak, not model speed; (c) batch size small; (d) generation could stream (red herring for rerank time).
  4. How I'd verify each: Plot recall@k of the gold chunk by stage-one rank; measure rerank time vs candidates; check queue depth.
  5. Root cause: Work is candidates x tokens; 200 x 450 per query at 40 QPS saturates the GPU and adds queueing.
  6. Fix: 50 candidates, truncation, larger batches, a smaller reranker, score cache for repeated queries, skip reranking when stage one has a clear winner, stream the generation.
  7. Prevention: Latency budget per stage in dashboards, eval run on every config change.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not dropping reranking blindly; not trusting the truncation without re-running the eval.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quality drops 0.03 at 50 candidates. → Try 100 with a smaller model, or improve stage one with hybrid.
  • Traffic doubles. → Autoscale GPU replicas, or use a hosted rerank API.
  • Queries repeat 30 percent. → Cache top-k by normalized query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found 97 percent of gold chunks were in the first 40 candidates; cutting 200 to 40 gave a 5x rerank speedup with no measurable loss.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes reranking or only scales hardware.
  • Hire: reduces candidates and length, verifies with eval.
  • Strong hire: uses recall-by-rank data, batching, conditional rerank, caching, and a budget per stage.

questions.contextHtml: A multi-tenant RAG service uses an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index of 50M chunks. The code retrieves top-10 and then removes chunks not belonging to the caller's tenant. Large tenants work fine. A small tenant (12k chunks, 0.02 percent of the index) reports "no results" for 40 percent of queries, though documents about the topic exist. Latency is normal. The team suspects the embedding model.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames embeddings or raises top-k to 50 without understanding the filter order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the filter applied before or after the ANN search? What does the DB do with filtered queries? Does the tenant's data exist in the index?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Over-fetch (top-1000) for small tenants as a stopgap, or route them to a dedicated collection.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) post-filtering: the global top-10 almost never contains the tenant's chunks (likely); (b) tenant data missing from ingestion; (c) wrong embedding model for that tenant (red herring: others work); (d) ANN recall parameters.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query with the tenant filter pushed into the DB and compare; count tenant chunks in the global top-1000.
  5. Root cause: With 0.02 percent selectivity, only about 2 in 10,000 results belong to the tenant, so top-10 then filter returns nothing.
  6. Fix: Use index-native filtered search (filter applied during graph traversal), partition or shard by tenant, or per-tenant collections for small tenants; for very selective filters a brute-force scan over the 12k chunks is cheap.
  7. Prevention: Test recall under realistic filter selectivity; alert on empty-result rate per tenant.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not increasing global top-k permanently (cost, and still fails for tiny tenants).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Native filtering is slow for tenants with 1 percent selectivity. → Check filter-aware index parameters or partitioning.
  • Filter plus ACL groups is complex. → Precompute allowed-group ids as a keyword array field.
  • Security implication of over-fetching? → Fine only if filtered before returning; never return other tenants' data to app code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "search is broken" ticket from the smallest customer was traced to post-filtering after the largest customer onboarded and diluted the global top-k.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model.
  • Hire: identifies post-filtering and proposes native filtering.
  • Strong hire: quantifies selectivity, offers partitioning/brute force options, adds per-tenant monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: Compare multi-query expansion and question decomposition. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Both involve extra LLM calls; interviewers want to see you pick the right one and know the cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Multi-query asks the model for several paraphrases of the same question, retrieves for each and merges (e.g. with RRF); it widens recall for one information need. Decomposition splits a complex question into sub-questions, each with different evidence, and combines the answers; needed when the answer needs several facts. Use paraphrasing for vocabulary mismatch, decomposition for multi-part questions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: "Compare the refund policy and warranty terms for the X200." Multi-query would give three phrasings of the same compare question and still might miss one document. Decomposition: (1) X200 refund policy, (2) X200 warranty terms, retrieve for each, then synthesize.

Sequential decomposition: later sub-questions depend on earlier answers ("who owns service A" then "on-call for that team"); that is multi-hop, so the retrieval must be run step by step.

Costs: extra LLM latency (200 ms to 2 s), more retrieval calls (parallelize independent ones), duplicates across lists (dedupe), and the risk of sub-questions drifting. Use an LLM only when a cheap classifier says the query is complex.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying decomposition to every query.
  • Not deduplicating before the reranker.
  • Generating 10 paraphrases that add no diversity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to merge results? → RRF then rerank against the original question.
  2. How to bound cost? → Cap sub-queries (e.g. 3), parallelize, cache.
  3. How to evaluate? → Per-question-type recall on a labelled complex-question set.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "generate more queries." Senior: distinguishes recall expansion from evidence decomposition and applies it conditionally.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Comparison questions failed on single-shot retrieval; splitting into per-entity sub-queries fixed most of them.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide when retrieval did not find enough evidence, so the system should say "I don't know" instead of answering?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hallucination often comes from forcing an answer from irrelevant context.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Always passing the top-k to the model means the model sees something even when nothing relevant exists. I use reranker scores, which are better separated than raw cosine, to set a threshold: if the best score is below it, or there is no clear gap, the bot declines or asks a clarifying question. I tune the threshold on labelled answerable and unanswerable queries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Raw cosine values depend on the embedding model and corpus (0.78 might be great in one and mediocre in another). Cross-encoder scores are trained to rank relevance, so a threshold is more stable, though still not a probability unless calibrated.

Method: build a set with answerable and out-of-scope questions. Plot score distributions of the top-1 chunk for each. Choose a threshold at your desired precision/recall trade-off (cost of a wrong answer vs a refusal). Also consider the gap between top-1 and top-2 and the number of chunks above threshold. Re-calibrate whenever the reranker, corpus or chunking changes.

Follow-through in the prompt: when evidence is weak, instruct the model to say what is missing, and offer related topics.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a cosine threshold copied from a blog post.
  • Never testing out-of-scope questions.
  • Treating the score as a probability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Threshold drifts after a model upgrade? → Re-fit on the eval set; keep the set versioned.
  2. Better than a threshold? → Add an LLM groundedness check, or a trained abstention classifier.
  3. Cost of false refusals? → Measure both error types and choose per product risk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "if similarity is low, say I don't know." Senior: calibrates on labelled answerable/unanswerable data, monitors drift, and balances the two errors.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legal assistant that always answered produced confident wrong clauses on out-of-scope questions until an abstention threshold was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A pgvector-backed endpoint serves 3 tenants. A security test with a canary document owned by tenant B shows it appears in tenant A's answers about 1 in 20 queries. Logs show correct tenant_id in the request token. Here is the retrieval code:

def search(conn, qvec, tenant_id, k=8):
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, text, tenant_id FROM chunks ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT %s",
        (qvec, k * 5),
    ).fetchall()
    hits = [r for r in rows if r[2] == tenant_id][:k]
    return hits + cache_get(qvec)   # cache keyed by embedding of the query
questions.promptHtml: Find all the problems and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only notices the post-filter and not the cache, or proposes adding "never reveal other tenants" to the prompt.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does cache_get return and how is it keyed? Is there row-level security? Any other path (admin, tools) that reads chunks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the cache path and put a feature flag to pause the endpoint for affected tenants; purge the cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the cache returns other tenants' chunks, keyed only by query embedding (likely, matches the intermittent pattern); (b) post-filter also gives too few results for small tenants (second bug); (c) request token parsing (red herring, logs are correct).
  4. How I'd verify each: Query as tenant A with the canary query and print the source of each hit; inspect cache keys.
  5. Root cause: The filter is applied in app code only to the DB rows, while cached results are appended unfiltered; also the cache key lacks tenant scope.
  6. Fix: Push the filter into SQL, scope the cache by tenant.
  7. Prevention: Postgres row-level security keyed by a session variable, canary tests in CI for every endpoint and cache, audit logging of chunk ids.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not relying on the prompt; not just shortening the cache TTL.

Fix (SQL pushed into the query, cache scoped):

def search(conn, qvec, tenant_id, k=8):
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, text FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = %s "
        "ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT %s",
        (tenant_id, qvec, k),
    ).fetchall()
    return rows   # cache key must be (tenant_id, normalized query)
fun search(conn: java.sql.Connection, qvec: String, tenantId: String, k: Int = 8): List<Pair<Long, String>> =
    conn.prepareStatement(
        "SELECT id, text FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector LIMIT ?"
    ).use { ps ->
        ps.setString(1, tenantId); ps.setString(2, qvec); ps.setInt(3, k)
        ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> generateSequence { if (rs.next()) rs.getLong(1) to rs.getString(2) else null }.toList() }
    }
static List<String> search(Connection conn, String qvec, String tenantId, int k) throws SQLException {
    String sql = "SELECT text FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector LIMIT ?";
    try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
        ps.setString(1, tenantId); ps.setString(2, qvec); ps.setInt(3, k);
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) { while (rs.next()) out.add(rs.getString(1)); }
        return out;
    }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Filtered ANN index returns fewer rows. → Check index type and ef_search/iterative scan options for your pgvector version (verify docs), or partition per tenant.
  • Shared documents between tenants? → Use ACL arrays or a join table instead of one tenant column.
  • Was data exposed? → Use audit logs of chunk ids per response to scope the incident.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A semantic cache keyed by query text was added for cost; two weeks later a canary test caught it serving one customer's answer to another.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests prompt instructions.
  • Hire: finds the post-filter and cache and moves the filter to SQL.
  • Strong hire: adds RLS, tenant-scoped cache, canary CI, audit, and incident scoping.

questions.promptHtml: A chunk says "The limit is 30 days." and nothing else. How do you make such chunks retrievable, and how does contextual retrieval compare with semantic chunking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Context loss at chunk boundaries is a root cause of many retrieval failures.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The chunk has lost its subject; neither "refund" nor the product appears. Contextual retrieval has an LLM write a one-sentence context for each chunk ("From the 2024 EU refund policy, section on opened items") and prepends it before embedding and BM25 indexing. Semantic chunking changes where I cut (by topic shifts), but does not restore context that sits outside the chunk. They address different problems and can be combined.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost: one LLM call per chunk at ingestion, bounded by passing the whole document (cached with prompt caching where supported) plus the chunk; a one-off cost, repeated when documents change. Benefit: both dense and BM25 indexes gain document-level terms. Anthropic reported a substantial reduction in failed retrievals with this approach (verify exact numbers in the original post).

Semantic chunking: embed sentences and cut when similarity between neighbors drops; yields coherent variable-size chunks but costs extra compute, and the quality gain over a good recursive split with overlap is not guaranteed; measure.

Alternatives: prepend the title/heading path cheaply (no LLM), parent-document retrieval, late chunking.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Spending on an LLM pass before trying heading-path prefixes.
  • Letting the generated context contain hallucinated facts.
  • Not re-generating context when the document changes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to cut cost? → Cheaper model, caching the document prefix, only for ambiguous chunks.
  2. Does the displayed text include the context? → Usually only used for indexing; store original text separately.
  3. How to prove it helps? → Recall@k on a labelled set before/after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use better chunk sizes." Senior: diagnoses lost context, applies the cheapest fix first, and quantifies ingestion cost vs recall gain.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Policy chunks with bare numbers were never retrieved until a heading-path prefix was added; the LLM context step then handled the remaining cases.

questions.contextHtml: An engineering-knowledge assistant uses hybrid retrieval + rerank (top 5). On 300 labelled questions, simple lookups score 88 percent correct, but "relationship" questions such as "Which team owns the service that caused the March 3 outage, and who is on call for it?" score 31 percent (about 90 of the 300 are this type). Each fact sits in a different document (incident report, service catalog, on-call schedule). Product wants a fix in 3 weeks. Someone proposes building a full knowledge graph.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Jumps to GraphRAG without checking that the failures are about connecting evidence, or increases top-k only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many hops typically (2 or 3)? Are entities consistently named? Is structured data (service catalog, on-call API) available? Latency budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise nothing yet; first inspect failures: is evidence 1 retrieved but 2 and 3 missing?
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the second and third facts need information from the first result, which the original query lacks (most likely); (b) on-call data is better fetched via API than retrieval; (c) entity-name mismatch between sources; (d) generator weakness (red herring if gold docs are present).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute recall of all gold documents per question; check in how many failures the first hop was found.
  5. Root cause: One-shot retrieval embeds the original question once; later hops need entities discovered in earlier hops.
  6. Fix: Iterative retrieval with a step cap of 3: retrieve, extract entities, issue the next query; for on-call, call the schedule tool. Log each step.
  7. Prevention: Keep the multi-hop eval set as a regression suite; track steps and cost per question.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No full knowledge graph in 3 weeks: high build and freshness cost, extraction errors; reconsider if iterative retrieval still fails on a measured class.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Latency 4 s now. → Parallelize independent hops, stream, cheaper model for planning.
  • Agent loops forever. → Step cap, stop condition, dedupe queries.
  • Corpus-wide "main themes" questions appear. → That is where community summaries or hierarchical summaries (RAPTOR/GraphRAG) can justify themselves.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team built a graph for a year; a 3-step retrieval loop plus two API tools later matched its accuracy on the production question mix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases top-k or proposes a graph unprompted.
  • Hire: diagnoses multi-hop and proposes iterative retrieval or decomposition.
  • Strong hire: diagnoses from data, uses tools for structured facts, bounds cost, and states when a graph is justified.

questions.promptHtml: What does GraphRAG do differently from vector RAG, what questions is it for, and what does it cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Graph approaches are hyped; interviewers want judgment about when they pay off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Vector RAG finds passages similar to the question. GraphRAG first has an LLM extract entities and relationships from the corpus into a graph, groups related entities into communities, and summarizes each. It then answers using relationship traversal or community summaries. It shines on corpus-wide questions ("what are the main themes?") and relationship questions; it is expensive to build and keep fresh.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pipeline: chunk, LLM-extract (entity, relation, entity) triples, build the graph, run community detection, summarize communities (hierarchically). Query modes: local (start from entities in the query, walk neighbors, gather text) and global (map-reduce over community summaries).

Why vector search fails on global questions: no single chunk contains "themes"; top-k sees a tiny sample. Costs: many LLM calls at indexing (scales with corpus size), extraction errors that propagate (wrong or duplicate entities), re-indexing on updates, harder debugging. Alternatives first: hybrid + rerank, multi-hop iterative retrieval, hierarchical summaries (RAPTOR), or SQL/API tools for structured joins.

Adopt when evaluation shows a significant class of real questions failing and cheaper methods do not fix it.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building the graph before measuring failures.
  • Ignoring entity resolution (the same service named three ways).
  • Forgetting incremental updates and permissions on graph nodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Local vs global search? → Entity neighborhood vs map-reduce over community summaries.
  2. Where do ACLs go? → On source chunks and propagated to derived nodes and summaries; summaries can leak.
  3. Cheaper than GraphRAG? → Hierarchical summaries or a graph from existing structured metadata.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "graph of entities for better answers." Senior: names the query classes it helps, its build and freshness costs, and cheaper alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A compliance team used community summaries for portfolio-wide risk questions but kept hybrid RAG for clause lookup.

questions.contextHtml: After shipping an LLM query-expansion step (generates 4 paraphrases, retrieves for each, RRF-merges), the live thumbs-up rate fell from 78 percent to 71 percent in a week. Offline eval on the 500-query set shows recall@10 rose from 0.84 to 0.88. Latency p95 went up 900 ms. Complaints mention "answers about the wrong product". The corpus has many near-identical product manuals (same text, different model numbers).
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Trusts the offline recall number and blames users, or reverts without understanding.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the eval set include model-number queries? Are paraphrases dropping model numbers? Are results reranked against the original query?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag the expansion off for queries containing model numbers/identifiers, or roll back to 10 percent traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) paraphrases drop or generalize the model number, so near-identical manuals of other models enter the fused list (likely); (b) the eval set lacks such queries, so recall@10 looks good; (c) latency hurts satisfaction; (d) generator change (red herring: none shipped).
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the paraphrases for failing sessions; segment thumbs-down by query type; replay on an eval slice with model numbers.
  5. Root cause: Expansion improved generic recall but caused drift away from the exact constraint (model number), and RRF rewards documents appearing across paraphrases, which favors generic manuals.
  6. Fix: Instruct the rewriter to preserve identifiers verbatim; apply metadata filters extracted from the query (model = X); rerank all candidates against the original query; weight the original query higher in fusion.
  7. Prevention: Eval set mirrors production mix (add identifier queries); online A/B before full rollout; log original vs transformed queries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not removing expansion everywhere, it helped other segments; not adding more paraphrases.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Latency still +900 ms. → Run in parallel, use a smaller model, or apply only when first-stage confidence is low.
  • Metadata extraction wrong? → Fall back to unfiltered search when the extractor confidence is low.
  • How to detect drift automatically? → Embedding similarity between original and paraphrase plus identifier-preservation checks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An offline metric rose while users complained; the cause was the eval set having none of the long-tail identifier queries that produce most complaints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts offline recall and ships or reverts without analysis.
  • Hire: finds drift on identifiers and segments the results.
  • Strong hire: fixes with filters, rerank on the original, representative eval, and staged rollout.

questions.contextHtml: You inherit a RAG system with a pipeline of dense retrieval, HyDE, multi-query (4), hybrid fusion, an LLM reranker over 100 candidates and a GraphRAG index. Cost per query is $0.06, p95 is 6.5 s, and the end-to-end correctness is 0.79. Nobody knows which parts matter. Budget goal: p95 under 2.5 s and cost under $0.02 with at most a 0.02 drop in correctness. You have a 600-question labelled set and two weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How do you simplify without wrecking quality?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Removes components by gut feeling or keeps everything because "each was added for a reason".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Query mix (lookup vs multi-hop vs global)? Is the eval representative and sliced by type? Which parts are shared with other products?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for quality; first add per-stage latency and cost logging.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) hybrid + a cheap cross-encoder gives most of the gain; (b) HyDE and multi-query help a few query types and hurt others; (c) the LLM reranker is the main cost; (d) GraphRAG helps only a small global-question segment.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ablation grid: remove one component at a time, then build up from a baseline of hybrid + rerank; report recall@k, correctness, latency, cost, sliced by query type, with confidence intervals (600 questions give noisy small slices).
  5. Root cause: Components were added without measurement, so cost accumulated.
  6. Fix: Keep baseline hybrid + small cross-encoder on 50 candidates; add conditional routing: expansions only for low-confidence or complex queries; graph only for classified global questions.
  7. Prevention: Each new component requires an eval win on a named query class and a budget line.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not deleting the graph before checking the segment it serves; not tuning on the final eval set repeatedly (overfitting), keep a held-out set.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two components each help only 1 point. → Compare cost per point and drop the more expensive.
  • Slice has 20 questions. → Treat as indicative; collect more data.
  • Router errors? → Measure router accuracy and default to the cheap path.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An ablation showed a 100-candidate LLM reranker improved correctness by 0.004 over a small cross-encoder at 10x the cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes components without data.
  • Hire: runs ablations on the eval set and reports cost and latency.
  • Strong hire: slices by query type, routes conditionally, guards against overfitting and sets a component admission rule.

questions.promptHtml: Compare a fixed retrieval pipeline with an iterative or agentic retrieval loop. What controls do you put around the loop?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Agentic retrieval is flexible but unpredictable; seniors know how to bound it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A fixed pipeline does one retrieval, then generates. An agentic loop lets the model retrieve, check whether it has enough evidence, and issue a new query if not, until it is satisfied or hits a limit. It handles multi-hop and vague questions better but costs more, varies in latency, and is harder to debug. I bound steps, budget tokens, dedupe queries and log every step.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Loop: plan -> search (tool) -> read results -> decide: answer, refine query, or search another source. The search tool should be the same hybrid + rerank + ACL-filtered retriever, with the user's identity passed through every call.

Controls: max steps (e.g. 3 to 5), max total tokens, timeouts, a repeated-query detector, a final "answer with what you have and state the gaps" fallback, trace logging (query, results, decision) for debugging and eval, and tests for the stopping behavior. Use the loop only for query classes where a fixed pipeline fails; route simple lookups to the cheap path.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No step cap, causing runaway cost.
  • The loop accumulates every result in context, so tokens balloon.
  • Running tools with the service identity rather than the user's.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you evaluate? → End-to-end correctness plus steps, tokens and latency distributions.
  2. Fixed pipeline with decomposition instead? → More predictable; fine when sub-questions are known upfront.
  3. How do you make it faster? → Parallel independent searches, smaller planner model.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "let the agent search until it knows." Senior: bounds, traces, routes by complexity, and propagates permissions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent re-issued near-identical queries 9 times on an unanswerable question until a repeated-query check and a 4-step cap were added.

questions.contextHtml: A compliance assistant indexes policies; when v4 of a policy is published, v3 stays in the index. Users report that the bot quotes outdated limits ("transfer limit is 5,000") in about 12 percent of policy answers; the current limit is 10,000. Audit finds both v3 and v4 chunks often appear in the top-5 together, and the model picks either. Documents have version, status (published/superseded) and effective_date fields, but retrieval ignores them. Index is 2M chunks.
questions.promptHtml: Fix it and prevent a recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Tells the prompt "use the latest version" or re-embeds everything.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should users ever see old versions (audits, "what was the limit last year")? Is status updated automatically on publish? Are metadata fields reliably filled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a default filter status = published AND effective_date <= today, and delete or flag v3 chunks from the default search path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) superseded chunks are still searchable (clear from the audit); (b) status not updated for some documents; (c) the model cannot tell versions apart because chunks lack version text (red herring after the filter is fixed); (d) stale cache.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count chunks by status; run the 12 percent failing queries with and without the filter; check cached answers' dates.
  5. Root cause: Superseded content shared the index and ranked equally because the same wording makes near-identical embeddings.
  6. Fix: Index-native filter on status and effective date; point-in-time parameter for historical questions; on publish, atomically mark the old version superseded and invalidate caches.
  7. Prevention: Test that asks the known-changed limit; monitor the share of cited chunks that are superseded (target 0); add version and effective date into the displayed citation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not hard-deleting old versions if audit requires them; not relying on a prompt rule.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users need "limit as of last June". → Add an as-of date filter: effective_date <= asof < superseded_date.
  • Metadata missing on legacy docs. → Backfill from file names or reprocess; fail ingestion when required fields are missing.
  • Boost recent instead of filtering? → Boosting is a soft signal and still lets stale text in; filter for hard rules, boost for preferences.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A finance bot quoted an old fee schedule for a month because the new PDF was ingested but the old one never marked superseded.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: prompt-only fix.
  • Hire: filters on status and effective date at retrieval.
  • Strong hire: adds point-in-time queries, atomic publish, cache invalidation, ingestion validation and a staleness metric.
